newsitem.title: USA: Garcia Abrego drug trial moves into second week.
newsitem.headline: Garcia Abrego drug trial moves into second week.

text.p: The trial of accused drug kingpin Juan Garcia Abrego moves into its second week on Monday with more testimony expected about cocaine, corruption and cash.

Witnesses including convicted drug dealers and FBI agents will testify about an illicit empire that earned billions of dollars shipping cocaine from its base in northern Mexico to the United States starting in the mid-1980s.

Prosecutors say Garcia Abrego, a former cookie factory worker from Texas, was the ruthless leader of the so-called Gulf Cartel, which at one time transported up to a third of the cocaine used in the United States. His attorneys say they have the wrong man.

He was on the FBI's 10 Most Wanted list before his capture in January in Monterrey, Mexico, and deportation to Houston for prosecution on 22 counts of drug-trafficking, money-laundering and bribery. Garcia Abrego, 52, faces life in prison if convicted.

The biggest revelation in the trial's first week was that U.S. agents, despite more than three years of continous wiretapping of the cartel's phone conversations, have no recordings of Garcia Abrego or even the mention of his name on tape. The defence has hammered home that point at every opportunity.

There has been little testimony about Garcia Abrego's alleged connections to Mexican government officials, although prosecutors said in opening arguments the cartel paid out huge sums of money to buy protection and a former FBI agent testified that the drug empire was built on public corruption.

News reports have linked Garcia Abrego to Raul Salinas, the brother of former President Carlos Salinas, who is in jail in Mexico City on charges he ordered the 1994 assassination of a high ruling party official.
Whether any of that will come out is unknown, but most testimony so far has detailed the cartel's inner workings and drug agents' attempts to stop them.
Witnesses told of shadowy figures called Shano, Guero, Gringo, El Profe (short for professor) and El Senor who, as a form of protection, never used their real names.

Drug agents testified about the difficulties of maintaining wiretaps because the cartel insiders constantly changed phone numbers and residences as they shuffled money and cocaine between Mexico and the United States.

Moving into rented homes and apartments, the drug dealers would try to blend in to their surroundings. Witnesses told of a Houston house where the cartel members held a backyard barbecue in which guests sat outside drinking beer and watching their children play.
But while the meat smoked on the grill, several men put down their beers long enough to load 300 kilos of cocaine into a mobile home in the driveway.

Out in the street, FBI agents watched it all, then followed the mobile home to New York City where members of the cocaine ring were arrested and the drugs, wrapped in brown paper marked with the "Rolex" trademark, were seized.
Rolex is an expensive brand of watch in the legal world, but also the name the Gulf Cartel gave high-quality cocaine it got from the Cali drug cartel in Colombia, agents said.
The driver of the mobile home, Bill Hoffman, a middle-aged resident of a Dallas suburb before he got sentenced to 12 years in a federal penitentiary, explained the lure of the drug business.
He said he transported marijuana for the cartel for several years by driving rental cars filled with pot from Texas to Florida. In 1986, he was asked to deliver cocaine.
"I didn't really want to at the time because there was a lot of risk. But the money got to be too good," Hoffman said.
For each round-trip, or two days of driving, he earned $30,000.
